raw_result.answerability_rationale: The provided evidence directly compares ion-exchange resin families (polystyrene-divinylbenzene vs polymethacrylate and polyacrylic) for removal of a broad set of PFAS in drinking water, and explicitly discusses how contact time alters the relative importance of PFAS properties versus resin polymer matrix. Additional evidence describes contact-time-related limitations (competitive adsorption at prolonged contact) for PS-DVB resins in PFAS-contaminated aqueous solutions. Together, these support both resin-family comparisons and contact-time effects without requiring extrapolation beyond the described systems.

task_components.component_text: Extract and compare how different ion-exchange resin families perform for broad PFAS removal, using explicit evidence about the matrix (e.g., type of water or solution tested), the PFAS compounds or classes considered, and the performance endpoints used (e.g., removal extent, breakthrough behavior, or other reported outcomes), including any stated operating constraints and limitations on applicability.

Extract how contact time influences PFAS removal performance for the evaluated ion-exchange resin families, including any explicit evidence on how sufficient versus shorter contact times affect the observed endpoints, and describe any reported operating constraints or limitations related to contact time (such as diminishing returns, practical runtime limits, or matrix-dependent effects) without generalizing findings to universal PFAS treatment claims.

claim_groups.canonical_proposition: In drinking-water experiments with a broad suite of PFAS, polystyrene-divinylbenzene ion-exchange resins removed a larger fraction of PFAS to high levels than polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins over a 24-hour contact time, indicating strong resin-family effects on broad PFAS removal performance.
claim_groups.central_proposition: PS-DVB ion-exchange resins outperformed polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins for broad PFAS removal in drinking water at 24 h contact time, achieving >90% removal for more PFAS compounds.
claim_groups.full_rule: Award full credit if the answer states that in drinking-water experiments with multiple PFAS, polystyrene-divinylbenzene (PS-DVB) ion-exchange resins achieved high removal (>90%) for many or most of the tested PFAS over a 24-hour contact time, while polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins achieved >90% removal for less than half of the PFAS, explicitly attributing this difference to resin-family or polymer-matrix effects and clearly indicating that the matrix was drinking water and the endpoint was PFAS removal extent.
claim_groups.partial_rule: Award partial credit if the answer notes that PS-DVB resins performed better than polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins for PFAS removal in water, but omits the broad scope of PFAS tested, the 24-hour contact time, or the comparative nature of removal fractions, or if the matrix or endpoint is only implicitly described.
claim_groups.contradiction_rule: Mark as contradicting if the answer claims that polymethacrylate or polyacrylic resins achieved equal or greater high-level removal than PS-DVB resins under the described conditions, or denies that resin-family (polymer matrix) affected broad PFAS removal performance in the drinking-water experiments.

exact_spans.supports: Direct comparison showing that PS-DVB resins achieved >90% removal for all 35 tested PFAS in 24 h, whereas polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins achieved >90% removal for fewer than half of those PFAS, demonstrating resin-family performance differences and the endpoint of removal extent.

raw_result.reference_answer:
In drinking-water ion-exchange experiments targeting a broad suite of PFAS, resin family had a strong effect on removal performance when sufficient contact time was provided. The study "[SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=c8e71b4e131d473aba74b8410ec99f2b57070cf6ff6a89c0eac736e5c4bb88a2]" reported that all five tested polystyrene-divinylbenzene (PS-DVB) resins achieved more than 90% removal in 24 hours of 35 PFAS compounds, whereas polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins achieved greater than 90% removal for less than half of these compounds, indicating higher broad-PFAS removal performance for PS-DVB resins under the tested conditions in drinking water.

Contact time influenced which factors controlled removal. Initially, PFAS properties such as chain length, charge, and functional groups affected adsorption to ion-exchange resins. However, in the same drinking-water experiments, when contact time increased beyond 2 hours, the impact of these PFAS properties on removal became less pronounced and the resin polymer matrix became the critical factor for PFAS removal. Thus, at longer contact times, differences among resin families (e.g., PS-DVB vs polymethacrylate or polyacrylic) played a dominant role in determining removal outcomes for the tested PFAS mixture.

Additional evidence from PFAS-contaminated aqueous solutions shows that PS-DVB-based resins can achieve high removal rates for shorter-chain PFAS such as PFBA and PFBS. However, very prolonged contact times can introduce operating limitations: with PS-DVB-based ion-exchange resins, prolonged contact times greater than 48 hours have been reported to cause competitive adsorption between long- and short-chain PFAS, which displaces shorter-chain PFAS from binding sites on the resin and reduces removal efficiency. This indicates that while longer contact times can be beneficial up to a point—allowing the polymer matrix to control broad PFAS removal—very long contact times may lead to diminished performance for some PFAS subclasses in certain aqueous matrices.

Overall, within the specific drinking-water and PFAS-contaminated aqueous systems studied, PS-DVB ion-exchange resins showed stronger broad PFAS removal than polymethacrylate and polyacrylic resins at 24-hour contact times, and increasing contact time beyond about 2 hours shifted control from PFAS-specific properties to the resin polymer matrix. At the same time, for PS-DVB resins in PFAS-contaminated aqueous solutions, contact times exceeding 48 hours were associated with competitive adsorption effects that reduced removal efficiency for shorter-chain PFAS. These findings are specific to the tested resins, PFAS mixtures, and aqueous matrices and should not be interpreted as universal behavior for all PFAS treatment scenarios.
